topic_summary: Analysis of Hebrew's transformation from liturgical preservation to native daily speech (late 19th-20th century), examining whether the commitment 'Hebrew is a living language' constitutes a contested kernel with structurally different readings about what counts as occupying that commitment—liturgical recitation versus native generation.

key_entities: Hebrew language (liturgical corpus preserved across diaspora)
Yiddish/Ladino speakers (competing vernaculars in Jewish communities)
Modern Israeli state (institutional enforcement of Hebrew as national language)
key_tensions: Liturgical preservation (sacred text recitation) vs native generation (daily vernacular use)
Continuity claim (unbroken transmission) vs reconstruction claim (deliberate revival from dormancy)

axes.structural_delta: Hebrew occupies 'living language' commitment through continuous liturgical recitation and textual study across diaspora communities
axes.primary_observable: Frequency and context of Hebrew use in prayer, Torah study, rabbinic discourse; absence of native speakers
axes.selection_reason: First reading of contested kernel; represents millennium-long institutional reading

axes.structural_delta: Hebrew occupies 'living language' commitment only when native speakers generate novel utterances in daily contexts, not merely recite preserved texts
axes.primary_observable: Presence of native speakers; lexical innovation rate; use in non-liturgical domains (commerce, child-rearing, governance)
axes.selection_reason: Second reading of contested kernel; represents revivalist/modernist reading

axes.structural_delta: Hebrew's 'living' status derives from unbroken liturgical transmission that enabled (rather than opposed) vernacular reconstruction—both readings are complementary phases
axes.primary_observable: Institutional narratives treating revival as restoration rather than invention; educational curricula emphasizing continuity
axes.selection_reason: Third reading of contested kernel; represents synthesis/legitimation reading

axes.structural_delta: Hebrew's vernacular status achieved through deliberate state policy suppressing competing languages (Yiddish, Ladino, Arabic) in education and public life
axes.primary_observable: Language policy documents; school curriculum mandates; suppression of Yiddish theater/press in early Israeli state
axes.selection_reason: Independent axis: enforcement mechanism distinct from kernel readings; survives §3 pairwise test (different observable: policy coercion vs linguistic practice)

omegas.description: Does the revival's dependence on Arabic-speaking Mizrahi Jews (who provided native Semitic phonology/syntax intuitions) constitute a fourth reading where 'living' status derives from sister-language transfer rather than internal preservation or reconstruction?

The D1 strict-reachability break (liturgical corpus → vernacular innovation) may indicate the liturgical reading does NOT occupy the kernel continuously—if recitation without native generation constitutes dormancy, then 'living language' commitment was vacant 70 CE–1880s CE, making revival a new instantiation rather than continuity.

Do rabbinic authorities benefit from the liturgical reading, or does that reading predate beneficiary analysis (mountain-like inevitability of preservation)? Classification as rope vs mountain contested.

fracture_scan.notes: F03 detected: liturgical_reading classified as rope (beneficiary: rabbinic_authority) but may be mountain (preservation inevitable given diaspora conditions). Generated omega_beneficiary_collapse to bound this uncertainty. Kernel structure confirmed: three readings pass individually-holdable test and emit structurally different constraints (different victim sets, different ε sources).

commitment_system_recognition.kernel_description: The commitment 'Hebrew is a living language' stabilized across two millennia with contested occupancy—whether liturgical recitation alone sustains 'living' status or whether native vernacular generation is required.
commitment_system_recognition.authority_description: Rabbinic tradition grounds interpretive legitimacy in unbroken textual transmission; Zionist revivalists ground legitimacy in demonstrated native-speaker community and state institutional enforcement.

readings.commitment: Hebrew is living if continuously recited in sacred contexts, regardless of native speakers
readings.expected_structural_delta: No victim set (preservation does not suppress alternatives); low ε (ritual practice, not resource extraction); rope hypothesis (coordination around liturgical corpus)

readings.commitment: Hebrew is living only when native speakers generate novel utterances in daily vernacular contexts
readings.expected_structural_delta: Victim set includes competing vernaculars (Yiddish, Ladino); moderate ε (institutional resources redirected to Hebrew education); tangled_rope hypothesis (nation-building extraction)

readings.commitment: Hebrew's living status derives from unbroken transmission enabling reconstruction—liturgical and vernacular phases are continuous
readings.expected_structural_delta: No victim set (synthesis narrative); low ε (legitimation function, not resource extraction); scaffold hypothesis (bridges competing readings for political cohesion)

axiom_contradictions.basis: Liturgical reading holds that preserved recitation constitutes occupancy; native-daily reading holds that only generative vernacular use constitutes occupancy. No single linguistic framework can hold both 'recitation = living' and 'recitation ≠ living' simultaneously.
